title: Theorem 1.3 — Conditional Stability for Single Interior Measurement
text: The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. {\rm (Main Theorem)} {\it Let $d > 0$ and $\Omega _d := \{ x \in \Omega \, :\,  \operatorname {dist}(x,\,  \mathbb {R}^n \setminus \Omega ) > d\} $. Let $\gamma _1, \gamma _2$ be an admissible pair and $A, \rho , \gamma _1, \gamma _2, \omega ^2$ satisfy Assumptions 1,2,3, with $||A||_{W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )} \le \sigma ^{-1}$ and $||\gamma _k||_{W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )} \le \sigma ^{-1},\,  k=1,2$. Then there exist constants $C>0$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$ depending only on $\Omega $, $d$, $\sigma $, $g_1$ and the coefficients of $L_1$ such that \begin{equation}  \Vert \gamma _2-\gamma _1\Vert _{L^\infty (\Omega _d)} \le C\left(\Vert \gamma _2-\gamma _1\Vert _{L^\infty (\partial \Omega )} +\Vert u_2-u_1\Vert _{W^{2,1}(\Omega )}\right)^\alpha \end{equation} for any $g_2$ and $\gamma _2$ of an admissible pair $(\gamma _1,\,  \gamma _2)$. title: Theorem 1.4 — Some stability inequalities for hybrid inverse problems
text: Under certain smoothness conditions on the domain and boundary data, if two functions are bounded and Lipschitz, equal on the boundary, and share the same potential, then their difference in the interior is controlled by the difference of their corresponding solutions. The estimate involves a constant exponent and a multiplicative constant depending on various parameters. The bound is expressed in terms of Holder-type norms. This result provides stability for an inverse problem or parameter identification. Assume that $\Omega $ is of class $C^3$ and $f\in H^{5/2}(\Gamma )$ is non constant. Let $\omega \Subset \Omega $, $(\lambda ,\mu )\in \mathcal{J}$ and $\varrho >0$. Then, for any $(\mathfrak {a},\mathfrak {q}), (\tilde{\mathfrak {a}},\mathfrak {q})\in \mathcal{D}_{\lambda ,\mu }^\bullet $ so that $\mathfrak {q}\in C^{0,1}(\overline{\Omega })$, $\|  \mathfrak {a}\| _{C^{0,1}(\overline{\Omega })}\le \varrho $, $\|  \tilde{\mathfrak {a}}\| _{C^{0,1}(\overline{\Omega })}\le \varrho $ and $ \mathfrak {a}=\tilde{\mathfrak {a}}$ on $\Gamma $, we have, with $u_{\mathfrak {a}}=u_{\mathfrak {a},\mathfrak {q}}$ and $u_{\tilde{\mathfrak {a}}}=u_{\tilde{\mathfrak {a}}, \mathfrak {q}}$,\[  \| \mathfrak {a}-\tilde{\mathfrak {a}}\| _{C(\overline{\omega })}\le C\varrho ^{1-\gamma }\| u_{\mathfrak {a}}-u_{\tilde{\mathfrak {a}}}\| _{L^2(\Omega )}^{\gamma /3},  \]where $C=C(n,\Omega , \omega ,\lambda ,\mu , \mathfrak {q} ,f)$ and $0<\gamma =\gamma (n,\Omega , \omega ,\lambda ,\mu ,f)$ are constants.

title: TheoremSearch: convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation
text: convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with finitely many parameters and Gaussian noise attaining Cramer-Rao bound Maximum likelihood estimation achieves the lowest possible variance for parameter estimation when the noise is Gaussian. This optimality is defined by the Cramér-Rao lower bound. The bound represents the smallest achievable variance for an unbiased estimator. For white Gaussian noise with covariance sigma squared times the identity matrix, the Cramer-Rao bound is at least N theta times sigma squared divided by two times the squared two-norm of M. Equality holds if the derivative of h sub M p with respect to theta, conjugated and multiplied by M conjugate transpose M over the squared norm of M and then by the derivative of h sub M p, equals the derivative of h sub M p conjugate transpose multiplied by the derivative of h sub M p. The Cramer-Rao lower bound applies to an unbiased estimator of a normalized signal parameter from noisy linear measurements. The noise is Gaussian with independent entries of known variance. The parameter is defined by scaling the signal by the sign of its last nonzero element. The estimator's covariance matrix minus the inverse Fisher information is positive semidefinite for parameters in the interior of the domain. The maximum likelihood estimator converges almost surely to the true parameter. The asymptotic distribution of the normalized estimation error is Gaussian. The covariance matrix of the limit distribution depends on the noise variance and the true parameter. The convergence rate is on the order of one over the square root of the sample size.

author: literature
title: Theorem 21 — Saving phase: Injectivity and stability for phase retrieval
text: The Cramer-Rao lower bound applies to an unbiased estimator of a normalized signal parameter from noisy linear measurements. The noise is Gaussian with independent entries of known variance. The parameter is defined by scaling the signal by the sign of its last nonzero element. The estimator's covariance matrix minus the inverse Fisher information is positive semidefinite for parameters in the interior of the domain. For $x\in \mathbb {R}^M$, let $Y=\mathcal{A}(x)+Z$ denote noisy intensity measurements with $Z$ having independent $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma ^2)$ entries. Furthermore, define the parameter $\theta $ to be $x$ divided by the sign of its last nonzero entry; let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {R}^{M}$ denote all such $\theta $. Then for any unbiased estimator $\hat{\theta }(Y)$ of $\theta $ in $\Omega $ with a finite $M\times M$ covariance matrix $C(\hat{\theta })$, we have $C(\hat{\theta })-J(\theta )^{-1}$ is positive semidefinite whenever $\theta \in \operatorname {int}(\Omega )$.

title: Theorem 2 — Theoretical Guarantees for AOA-based Localization: Consistency and Asymptotic Efficiency
text: The maximum likelihood estimator converges almost surely to the true parameter. The asymptotic distribution of the normalized estimation error is Gaussian. title: TheoremSearch: Convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares pa
text: Convergence of Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt for finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares parameter identification with Lipschitz stable forward map The Gauss-Newton method converges to a solution for a nonlinear least squares problem under certain conditions. The method is well-defined and the sequence remains within a ball around the solution. The convergence rate is bounded by an expression involving the initial error and a function f. The radius of convergence is optimal under additional equality conditions, and the solution is unique under a further hypothesis. title: Theorem 18 — Local convergence analysis of Gauss-Newton's method under majorant condition
text: For a continuously differentiable function F from an open set in R^n to R^m with m at least n, assume x_* is a solution where F' has full rank and satisfies a Lipschitz condition. Under a specific bound involving constants c, beta, and K, the Gauss-Newton method with initial point near x_* is well-defined, remains in a ball around x_*, and converges to x_*. The convergence is quadratic-linear with an explicit error bound. The radius r is the best possible under a given inequality, and x_* is the unique solution in a certain ball if an additional condition holds. Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb {R}^{n}$ be an open set, $F:{\Omega }\to \mathbb {R}^{m}$ be continuously differentiable in $\Omega $ and $m\geq n$. Let $x_* \in \Omega $ and\[ c:=\| F(x_*)\| ,\qquad \beta :=\| [F'(x_*)^TF'(x_*)]^{-1}F'(x_*)^T\| , \qquad \kappa :=\sup \left\{  t\in [0, R): B(x_*, t)\subset \Omega \right\} .  \]Suppose that $x_*$ is a solution of \eqref{eq:p1}, $F '(x_*)$ has full rank and there exists a $K>0$ such that\[  \sqrt{2}c\beta ^2 K<1, \qquad \qquad \left\| F'(x)-F'(y)\right\|  \leq K\| x-y\| , \qquad \forall \;  x, y\in B(x_*, \kappa ). \]Let\[ r:=\min \left\{ \kappa ,\, \big(2-2\sqrt{2}K\beta ^2c\big)/\big(3K\beta \big)\right\} . \]Then, the Gauss-Newton methods for solving \eqref{eq:p1}, with initial point $x_0\in B(x_*, r)/\{ x_*\} $\[  x_{k+1}={x_k}- \left[F'(x_k)^TF'(x_k)\right]^{-1}F'(x_k)^TF(x_k), \qquad \;  k=0,1,\ldots .  \]is well defined, the sequence generated $\{ x_k\} $ is contained in $B(x_*,r),$ converges to $x_*$ and\[  \| x_{k+1}-x_*\|  \leq \frac{\beta K}{2(1-\beta K\| x_0-x_*\| )}\| x_k-x_*\| ^2+\frac{\sqrt{2}c \beta ^2K}{1-\beta K\| x_0-x_*\| }\| x_k-x_*\| , \qquad \;  k=0,1,\ldots .  \]Moreover, if $(2-2\sqrt{2}K\beta ^2c)/(3K\beta )<\kappa $, then $r=(2-2\sqrt{2}K\beta ^2c)/(3K\beta )$ is the best possible convergence radius.\\ If, additionally, $2c\beta _0K<1,$ then the point $x_*$ is the unique solution of \eqref{eq:p1} in $B(x_*,(2-2c\beta _0K)/(\beta K))$, where $\beta _0:=\| [F'(x_*)^TF'(x_*)]^{-1}\| $.

text:
Under certain assumptions on the Jacobian mapping, gradient descent with a specific step size applied to a non-linear least squares problem yields geometric convergence of the residual. The residuals of the original and linearized problems remain close throughout all iterations. The parameters of both problems also stay close to each other. Additionally, the parameters remain within a bounded distance from the initial point. Assume the Jacobian mapping $\mathcal J(\bm \theta )\in \mathbb R^{n\times N}$ associated with the function $f(\bm \theta )$ obeys Assumptions \ref{BndSpec}, \ref{assJac2}, and \ref{assJac3} around an initial point $\bm \theta _0\in \mathbb R^N$ with respect to a reference Jacobian $\mathbf J\in \mathbb R^{n\times N}$ and with parameters $\alpha , \beta , \epsilon _0, \epsilon $, obeying $2\beta (\epsilon _0 + \epsilon ) \leq \alpha ^2$, and $R$. We run gradient descent with stepsize $\eta \leq \frac{1}{\beta ^2}$ on the linear and non-linear least squares problem, starting from the same initialization $\bm \theta _0$. Then, for all iterations $t$,\begin{enumerate} \item[i)]the non-linear residual converges geometrically 

\begin{align}  \label{resnl} {\left\| \mathbf r_{t}\right\| }_{2}\le \left(1-\eta \alpha ^2\right)^t {\left\| \mathbf r_0\right\| }_{2}, \end{align}

\item[ii)]the residuals of the original and the linearized problems are close 

\begin{align}  {\left\| \mathbf r_t- \widetilde{\mathbf r}_t\right\| }_{2} & \leq 2 \beta \eta (\epsilon _0 + \epsilon )(1 - \eta \alpha ^2)^{t-1} t{\left\| \mathbf r_0\right\| }_{2} \label{eq:propvrkclose}\\

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Learned initializer + Gauss-Newton/LM refinement with posterior-mean estimator reaches the CRB regime
text: A kernel-ridge amortized initializer followed by bounded LM refinement in log-k through the exact forward model, reported as the importance-sampled posterior mean under the box prior, achieves val rel_l2 < 0.03. That is within ~1.5x of the CRB floor of 0.0195 and well below the 0.05 success threshold. A purely data-driven regressor of comparable cost will be at least 30% worse. The forward map theta -> u(x_s, t_n) is smooth in k on [0.5,2]^4 and cheap (40 nodes, 200 explicit steps). Noise is tiny (sigma=1e-3) relative to the signal. The median Fisher condition number of 46.6 means the Gauss-Newton normal matrix is well-conditioned and full rank. In this regime the local least-squares estimator is asymptotically efficient, so per-sample inversion should approach the CRB. The main failure mode of pure LM is a poor start; an amortized regressor trained on 3000 simulated pairs gives starts inside the basin. The posterior mean minimises expected squared error. It also handles the box edges where k1 and k4 (least determined, CRB rel std about 2%) may be truncated by the bounds, which a clipped MLE handles poorly. The log transform matches positivity and the scale-like role of k in the diffusion time ~ L^2/k. The harness forward model is the same simulator that generated train/val/test, so there is no model discrepancy. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=1e-3, so the LM objective is the exact negative log-likelihood up to constants. The Jacobian is full rank across the prior box, extrapolated from the harness Fisher diagnostics at 32 draws. Kernel ridge initial error (expected rel_l2 ~0.05-0.15) lies inside the Gauss-Newton convergence basin. The explicit scheme is stable for k<=2 (dt*k/dx^2 <= 1/2) as configured by the harness; otherwise forward outputs would be nonsmooth.

assumptions: The harness forward model is the same simulator that generated train/val/test, so there is no model discrepancy.
Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=1e-3, so the LM objective is the exact negative log-likelihood up to constants.
The Jacobian is full rank across the prior box, extrapolated from the harness Fisher diagnostics at 32 draws.
Kernel ridge initial error (expected rel_l2 ~0.05-0.15) lies inside the Gauss-Newton convergence basin.
The explicit scheme is stable for k<=2 (dt*k/dx^2 <= 1/2) as configured by the harness; otherwise forward outputs would be nonsmooth.
data.falsifiable_test: Evaluate val rel_l2. The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 >= 0.03, or if the best library method on the same features is within 30% of it. A secondary check: the median per-sample GN-predicted std should be within a factor of 1.5 of the CRB values, which would show the refinement is efficient rather than merely lucky.
data.if_fails: If rel_l2 stalls near the initializer's error, LM is not converging: either the Jacobian is effectively rank-deficient in parts of the box (e.g. k1/k4 weakly sensed) or the forward model differs from the data generator, which we can check via residual norms vs sigma*sqrt(m). If the result is about 0.03-0.05 with residuals at the noise level, the CRB estimate from 32 draws understates average difficulty, and posterior_mean vs mode should be compared.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Pure per-sample MLE with multistart LM (no learning) is sufficient: the least-squares landscape is effectively unimodal on the prior box
text: The misfit J(log k) = ||F(k) - y||^2 / sigma^2 has a single basin over [0.5,2]^4 for these sensors, apart from bound-truncation effects. Therefore physics-only bounded LM in log-space with 4 multistarts and no prior regularisation (MLE, mode estimator) achieves val rel_l2 < 0.035. It also lands within 20% of the hybrid in proposal 1, which shows the learned initializer buys compute but not accuracy. This is a structural claim about the inverse operator, not a tuning claim. In 1-D, each conductivity segment controls the effective diffusion time between the central pulse and the sensors. The sensors at indices 5, 15, 25, 35 each sit inside one of the four segments (assuming equal segments of 10 nodes), so each k_i has a dedicated, monotone-ish signature in the arrival and decay of its local sensor. That suggests F is close to injective with a monotone Jacobian structure, giving no spurious local minima. If true, multistart solutions should coincide, and accuracy is limited only by noise (CRB), not by optimisation. The MLE is not fully efficient near the box edges, so we predict a small gap to the posterior-mean hybrid that is not large. Segment boundaries are equal quarters, so each sensor lies inside a distinct segment. This is inferred from the indices; it is not stated. LM from the prior centre or random starts converges in <=30 iterations, given cond ~47. The forward model is identical to the data generator. Bound clipping in log space is handled by the harness's bounded LM.

data.falsifiable_test: The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 >= 0.035, or if it is more than 20% worse than the proposal-1 hybrid. Diagnostic: the fraction of val samples whose final scaled residual ||F(k_hat)-y||/(sigma*sqrt(m)) exceeds 1.2 (non-converged or local minimum) should be < 2%. A larger fraction indicates multimodality or poor convergence.
data.if_fails: If residuals are near the noise level but rel_l2 is high, the error is noise amplification at weakly sensed k1/k4. That would point to MAP/posterior_mean (tikhonov>0) being necessary and to the box prior carrying real information. If residuals are high for some samples, the landscape is multimodal or LM stalls, which justifies the learned initializer in proposal 1. Either outcome sharpens the identifiability picture.

author: researcher-ml
title: Learned initializer plus Gauss-Newton/LM refinement through the forward model reaches near-CRB accuracy
text: A cheap learned inverse map (kernel ridge on standardized raw sensor traces, log-target) followed by a few bounded Levenberg-Marquardt iterations in log-k space will reach test rel_l2 <= 0.035, within about 1.8x of the CRB floor (0.0195). Purely data-driven maps trained on 3000 samples will stay clearly above this. The diagnostics show the problem is locally well posed. The median Fisher condition number is 46.6, and per-parameter CRB relative std is 0.5 to 2%, so the MLE is informative. With sigma = 0.001, the likelihood is sharply peaked, which makes a Gauss-Newton step from a good initial point close to efficient. The main risk for pure LM is local minima or slow convergence from the prior centre in the poorly determined end segments (k1, k4). A learned initializer should land inside the basin, so LM only has to remove the residual bias and variance of the regressor. The log transform enforces positivity and roughly balances curvature across the [0.5, 2] range. context.forward is the same discretization that generated the data (explicit FD, 40 points, 200 steps), so there is no model error Noise is i.i.d. author: researcher-ml
title: Amortized MLP with log-target and noise augmentation is accurate but cannot reach the CRB without physics refinement
text: A torch MLP trained on raw standardized sensor traces, with log-conductivity targets and noise augmentation at the true sigma, will reach val/test rel_l2 in [0.04, 0.08]. That is well below the mean baseline (0.33), but at least 1.5x worse than the best physics or hybrid method, because 3000 training samples are too few to learn the inverse map near the CRB precision in 4-D. The inverse map from roughly 800 correlated sensor readings to 4 parameters is smooth but nonlinear. Diffusive smoothing makes it strongly correlated and close to low rank, so an MLP should capture it. Precision is the issue, not expressiveness: the CRB requires about 1% accuracy. An amortized regressor's error has an approximation/estimation term that decays slowly with n, and 3000 samples cover the 4-D box at roughly 7 points per dimension. Training on fresh noise draws at the true sigma should regularize the network toward the posterior-mean map rather than fitting to clean features. This experiment measures how much the forward model adds over pure learning. Training data is generated by the same simulator with the same noise level as the test data noise_aug adds Gaussian perturbations comparable to sigma = 0.001 in raw feature units Log targets make errors roughly relative, which aligns with rel_l2 CPU training of a [512, 256, 128] MLP for about 200 epochs on 3000 samples fits within 120 s

author: researcher-experimental
title: Noise-limited regime: bounded log-space MLE through the forward model should land near the CRB floor (~0.02 rel_l2)
text: The observation map is locally well-conditioned (Fisher condition number median 46.6) and sigma=0.001 is small relative to the signal. Most of the irreducible error should therefore come from measurement noise, not from model misfit or local minima. A per-sample bounded Levenberg–Marquardt MLE in log-k with a few multistarts should reach val rel_l2 within about 1.6x of the harness CRB floor (0.0195), i.e. below 0.032, clearing the 0.05 target. The competing explanation is non-convexity or multimodality of the misfit, especially in the weakly determined k1 and k4. If that is right, a large share of samples will converge to wrong basins and rel_l2 will stay well above the CRB, with a heavy-tailed per-sample error distribution. Training and test data come from the same known forward model: explicit FD, 40 points, 200 steps, known Gaussian initial condition, known i.i.d. noise. So the likelihood is exactly specified, with no simulation-fidelity gap. An exactly specified Gaussian likelihood with 4 parameters and many correlated time samples is the textbook setting where MLE approaches the CRB. A learned regressor trained on 3000 draws has to learn a 4-D inverse map from high-dimensional noisy features. That adds approximation and estimation error on top of the noise floor. The physics arm is the natural reference that every data-driven arm should be judged against. context.forward is the same simulator (grid, dt, IC, sensor indices) that generated the train/val/test features, so there is zero model discrepancy Noise is additive i.i.d. data.falsifiable_test: Run on the 750 val samples. Report overall rel_l2, per-parameter relative RMSE versus the CRB per-parameter std, and the fraction of samples whose final residual norm^2 exceeds the chi-square 99% quantile for the observation dimension (a wrong-basin indicator). The hypothesis is refuted if val rel_l2 >= 0.032, or if more than 5% of samples have residuals inconsistent with sigma=0.001, which would point to local minima or model mismatch rather than a noise limit.
data.if_fails: If residuals are chi-square-consistent but error is still above 1.6x CRB, the error comes from estimator bias or boundary effects, and an MMSE estimator (proposal 2) should help. If residuals are too large, we have local minima, so better initialization (a learned init) is the remedy. If even the best restarts misfit, the forward model does not match the data generator, which is a simulation-fidelity finding that would also undermine any physics-based arm.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Metric-matched estimator: a learned init plus LM refinement with a posterior-mean (MMSE) readout beats the MAP/MLE mode on rel_l2, mainly via k1 and k4 near the
text: rel_l2 is a squared-error metric, so under the known uniform box prior the Bayes-optimal point estimate is the posterior mean, not the mode. For the weakly determined k1 and k4, the posterior near the bounds 0.5 and 2.0 is truncated and skewed. The mode piles up on the bound or overshoots in log space, while the posterior mean shrinks correctly. The hybrid works in two steps. A cheap ridge regressor on log features gives a basin-correct initial guess, which removes the need for multistart. LM refinement plus importance-sampled posterior mean should then reach val rel_l2 at least 5% lower than the best pure-physics (mode) arm. The competing explanation is that the posterior is near-Gaussian and far from the bounds for almost all samples. In that case mean and mode coincide, and the gain will be under 2%, within seed noise. This is an evaluation-design argument: match the estimator to the loss. Because the prior and noise model are specified exactly, the posterior mean is computable and its benefit is directly testable against the mode. Using a learned initializer also tests a separate, data-distribution question: is a simple amortized map trained on 3000 simulated draws good enough to put LM in the right basin? If so, physics-grade accuracy can be reached with fewer forward solves than multistart needs. author: researcher-exploratory
title: Rel-L2 is a squared loss, so target the Bayes estimator: learned init, then LM refinement, then a posterior-mean (MMSE) estimate under the box prior
text: With a box prior and weakly determined end segments (k1, k4), the per-sample MAP/MLE is biased toward the bounds, and its error is inflated wherever the likelihood is flat. Two claims follow. (a) A hybrid that refines a torch_mlp initializer by log-space Levenberg-Marquardt and then reports the importance-sampled posterior mean will reach val rel_l2 <= 0.03, within about 1.5x of the CRB floor of 0.0195. (b) The same pipeline with estimator='mode' will be measurably worse on k1 and k4. The usual framing says 'find the parameters that fit the data' (MLE or MAP). But the metric is a mean squared relative error, which the posterior mean minimises under the stated prior. The CRB floor of 0.0195 is a bound for unbiased estimators only. A Bayes estimator that uses the uniform prior can beat it per-parameter where the bound is loose, especially for k1 and k4 (relative std 0.021 and 0.016) near the bounds 0.5 and 2.0. The learned initializer removes the multistart cost and the risk of local minima. Doing the LM in log space respects positivity and the multiplicative structure of k. The forward model in context.forward matches the data-generating simulator exactly: same explicit FD scheme, 40 nodes, 200 steps, same sensors. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 0.001, so the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation is a reasonable proposal for importance sampling. The posterior is unimodal near the MLP initializer. The Fisher condition number of about 47 suggests no severe ridge. The forward-call budget covers 750 val plus 750 test samples x (about 20 LM iterations + 256 posterior samples), using vectorised forward calls.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Amortised MMSE: a squared-loss network trained with noise augmentation is itself a posterior-mean estimator; test whether it reaches the target without any forw
text: A network trained with squared loss on prior-distributed simulations with matched sensor noise approximates E[k | data]. With only 3000 simulations, plus noise augmentation at the true sigma and a log-target transform, the amortised estimator will reach val rel_l2 < 0.05. It will remain at least 30% worse than the best hybrid, because limited simulations leave the approximation error above the Bayes risk. This challenges the assumption that per-sample physics inversion is needed. The 4-parameter map is smooth, the features are high-dimensional but highly redundant, and the noise is small relative to signal. Regression on simulations is amortised Bayesian inference: the regression function of a squared-loss learner is the posterior mean. The open question is whether 3000 draws in 4-D are enough. Four dimensions is low enough that the answer may be yes. Noise augmentation at the true sigma makes the learner see the correct likelihood, rather than overfit to single noise realisations. Raw features rather than log ones avoid amplifying additive noise where temperatures are near zero. The training features already contain sensor noise at sigma = 0.001. The harness's noise_scale is in units of the stated noise std, so augmentation adds fresh draws at the matched level. Prior draws cover [0.5, 2]^4 densely enough. 3000 points give roughly 7 points per axis on a grid, which is reasonable for a smooth map. The inverse map is smooth in log-k. This is plausible because the heat solution depends analytically on k.

data.falsifiable_test: Report val rel_l2 for this spec, and for the same spec with noise_aug=0, alongside the best hybrid's val rel_l2. The first claim is falsified if rel_l2 >= 0.05. The 'amortisation gap' claim is falsified if the MLP is within 30% of the best hybrid. The noise-augmentation claim is falsified if noise_aug=0 is equal or better.
data.if_fails: If it beats 0.05 and approaches the hybrid, amortised inference is sufficient and the forward-call budget is better spent generating more simulations than on per-sample LM. If it misses 0.05, simulation scarcity, not identifiability, is the bottleneck for data-driven methods. That justifies physics refinement or a custom_solver that simulates fresh training data through context.forward.

title: TheoremSearch: KRR-only val rel_l2 and per-parameter rel RMSE
text: KRR-only val rel_l2 and per-parameter rel RMSE The KRR estimator achieves an upper bound on the squared L2 error that decays with the sample size n, for a specific choice of the regularization parameter. The rate of decay depends on the parameters beta and p. A matching lower bound holds for all measurable learning methods, showing the rate is minimax optimal. The bounds hold with high probability under certain conditions. Two-step KRR is consistent. The inferred hypothesis converges to the true regression function. The convergence rate is at least proportional to the minimum of m and q raised to a negative power. The exponent depends on the smoothness parameters nu bar and nu. The mean squared error of the truncated kernel ridge regression estimator is bounded by a combination of terms involving lambda, r, and noise. For specific choices of lambda and r, TKRR achieves a convergence rate that depends on the noise variance, sample size, and parameters gamma and alpha. Under certain noise conditions, the full kernel ridge regression achieves a different optimal rate with a regularization parameter choice that depends on delta, which is the minimum of 1 and gamma. The rates for both estimators are expressed as powers of the ratio of noise variance to sample size. Given a fixed regression function in L2 space, under specific assumptions on smoothness parameters and function norms, the difference between the kernel ridge regression risk and the ridge regression risk is bounded. The bound holds with high probability as dimension increases. The error scales with logarithmic factors and terms involving dimension and sample size. The bound is relative to the ridge regression risk itself.

Suppose Assumption \ref{assump_asymptotic} and \ref{assu:coef_of_inner_prod_kernel} hold for some $\alpha , \gamma > 0$. Denote $\ell = \lfloor \gamma \rfloor $. title: Theorem 2 — Target alignment in truncated kernel ridge regression
text: The mean squared error of the truncated kernel ridge regression estimator is bounded by a combination of terms involving lambda, r, and noise. For specific choices of lambda and r, TKRR achieves a convergence rate that depends on the noise variance, sample size, and parameters gamma and alpha. Under certain noise conditions, the full kernel ridge regression achieves a different optimal rate with a regularization parameter choice that depends on delta, which is the minimum of 1 and gamma. The rates for both estimators are expressed as powers of the ratio of noise variance to sample size. Let $\eta = \min (r, \lambda ^{-1/\alpha })$. Under the polynomial decay assumption~\eqref {eq:poly:decay:assump}, \begin {align}\label {eq:poly:rate:mse} \mathbb{E} \|\widetilde f _{r,\lambda } - f^*  \|_n^2 \;\asymp \; \lambda ^2 \max (1 , \eta ^{-2(\gamma -1)\alpha }) + r^{-2\gamma \alpha } 1\{r < n\} + \frac {\sigma ^2}{n} \eta . \end {align} \begin {enumerate}[(a),wide] \item \label {part:tkrr:rate} Taking $\lambda \asymp (\sigma ^2/n)^{\gamma \alpha /(2\gamma \alpha +1)}$ and $r \asymp (n/\sigma ^2)^{1/(2\gamma \alpha +1)}$, TKRR achieves the following rate \begin {align}\label {eq:TKRR:optimal:rate} \mathbb{E} \|\widetilde f _{r,\lambda } - f^*  \|_n^2 \;\asymp \; \Bigl (\frac {\sigma ^2}{n}\Bigr )^{2\gamma \alpha /(2\gamma \alpha +1)} \quad \text {for $\gamma > 1$}. \end {align} \item \label {part:full:rate} Assume $n^{-2\alpha } \lesssim \sigma ^2 \lesssim n$, and let $\delta := \min (1,\gamma )$. Then, the best rate achievable by the full KRR is obtained for regularization choice $\lambda \asymp (\sigma ^2/n)^{\alpha /(2\delta \alpha + 1)}$ and is given by \begin {align}\label {eq:full:KRR:optimal:rate} \mathbb{E} \|\widetilde f _{r,\lambda } - f^*  \|_n^2 \;\asymp \; \Bigl (\frac {\sigma ^2}{n}\Bigr )^{2\delta \alpha /(2\delta \alpha +1)} \quad \text {for $\gamma > 0$}. \end {align} \end {enumerate}

title: Proposition 7.3 (Restate Theorem 2 in \cite{misiakiewicz2024non}) — On the Pinsker bound of inner product kernel regression in large dimensions
text: Given a fixed regression function in L2 space, under specific assumptions on smoothness parameters and function norms, the difference between the kernel ridge regression risk and the ridge regression risk is bounded. The bound holds with high probability as dimension increases. The error scales with logarithmic factors and terms involving dimension and sample size. The bound is relative to the ridge regression risk itself. Given a dimension $d$, let $f_{\star } \in L^2$ be a fixed regression function. Suppose Assumption \ref{assump_asymptotic} and \ref{assu:coef_of_inner_prod_kernel} hold for some $\alpha , \gamma > 0$. Denote $\ell = \lfloor \gamma \rfloor $. Suppose there exists a constant $C$, such that $\left\| \mathrm{P}_{>\ell } f_{\star }\right\| _{L^2} \geq \left\| f_{\star }\right\| _{L^2} / C$, and for any integer $q \geq 2$, we have $\left\| f_{\star }\right\| _{L^q} \leq (C q)^{(\ell +1) / 2}\left\| f_{\star }\right\| _{L^2}$. Then under certain conditions, with probability $1-o_d(1)$, we have\[  \left|R_{\text{KRR}}\left(f_{\star }, X, \lambda \right) - R_{\text{RR}}(\lambda _{\star })\right| = O_{d}\left(\log ^{3(\ell +2)}(d) \cdot \left(\sqrt{\frac{d^{\ell -1}}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{d^{\ell +1}}}\right)\right)R_{\text{RR}}(\lambda _{\star }).  \]

author: researcher-mathematical
title: TheoremSearch: Per-sample CRB at all 750 val truths: report mean and 90th percentile of the rel_l2 implied by the C
text: Per-sample CRB at all 750 val truths: report mean and 90th percentile of the rel_l2 implied by the CRB The relative error in the LQR cost is bounded by an expression involving system parameters and the number of data samples. This bound holds with high probability when the sample size is sufficiently large. The bound depends on the minimum eigenvalue of a certain matrix, noise variances, and the H-infinity norm of a closed-loop system. The constants in the bound are universal and do not depend on the specific system. The theorem establishes bounds on the deviation between estimated and true values. It states that the difference between the estimated and true mean is bounded by a constant times the square root of the sample size. Similarly, the L2 norm of the difference between estimated and true probability distributions is bounded by another constant times the square root of the sample size. The infinity norm of the log difference between these distributions is also bounded by a constant divided by the square root of the sample size. Under certain assumptions, the probability that the estimated variance of Y deviates from half to double the true variance decays at least as fast as n to the negative second power. The probabilities that several other sets fail also decay at least as fast as n to the negative second power. These bounds hold for all n greater than or equal to one. A numerical constant C exists such that these inequalities are valid. The probability that the absolute difference between the estimator and the true value exceeds a relative error bound decays exponentially with the sample size. This exponential decay rate depends on the square of the error tolerance and the square root of the true value. The bound holds for relative errors between zero and one. The result is non-asymptotic and provides a concrete concentration inequality.

title: Corollary 4.3 — On the Sample Complexity of the Linear Quadratic Regulator
text: The relative error in the LQR cost is bounded by an expression involving system parameters and the number of data samples. This bound holds with high probability when the sample size is sufficiently large. The bound depends on the minimum eigenvalue of a certain matrix, noise variances, and the H-infinity norm of a closed-loop system. The constants in the bound are universal and do not depend on the specific system. Let $\lambda _G = \lambda _{\min }(\sigma _u^2 G_TG_T^*+ \sigma _w^2 F_TF_T^*)$, where $F_T, G_T$ are defined in \eqref{eq:gramians}. Then there are universal constants $C_0$ and $C_1$ such that the relative error in the LQR cost satisfies\begin{align}   & \frac{J(A, B, \mathbf{K}) - J_\star }{J_\star } \leq C_0 \sigma _w \| \mathfrak {R}_{A+ BK_\star }\| _{\mathcal{H}_\infty }\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda _G}} + \frac{\|  K_\star  \| _2}{\sigma _u}\right)\sqrt{\frac{(n+ p)\log (1/\delta )}{N}} \end{align}with probability $1 - \delta $, as long as $N \geq C_1(n+ p)\sigma _w^2 \|  \mathfrak {R}_{A + BK_\star } \| _{\mathcal{H}_\infty }^2(1 / \lambda _G + \|  K_\star  \| _2^2/\sigma _u^2) \log (1/\delta )$.

title: Theorem 56 — Asymptotic properties and approximation of Bayesian logspline density estimators for communication-free parallel computing methods
text: The theorem establishes bounds on the deviation between estimated and true values. It states that the difference between the estimated and true mean is bounded by a constant times the square root of the sample size. Similarly, the L2 norm of the difference between estimated and true probability distributions is bounded by another constant times the square root of the sample size. The infinity norm of the log difference between these distributions is also bounded by a constant divided by the square root of the sample size. There exist constants $M_1$, $M_2$, $M_3$ and $M_4$ such that for all $\omega \in \Omega _{n}$\begin{equation}  \begin{aligned} &  |\hat{y}(\theta _1(\omega ),\dots ,\theta _n(\omega ))-\bar{y}| \leq \dfrac {M_{1}(L+1)}{\sqrt{n}}\\ &  \|  \hat{p}(\cdot ,\omega )-\bar{p}(\cdot )\| _{2} \leq M_{3}\sqrt{\dfrac {L+1}{n}}\\ &  \| \log (\hat{p}(\cdot ,\omega ))-\log (\bar{p}(\cdot ))\| _{\infty } \leq \dfrac {M_{4}(L+1)}{\sqrt{n}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}

text: Hold the initializer and LM settings fixed. Replacing the mode readout with the box-truncated k-space posterior mean then reduces val rel_l2 by a small but real amount, giving rel_l2 < 0.0195 in aggregate. Nearly all of the gain is concentrated in samples whose k1 or k4 truth lies within 2 GN-std of a bound. In the interior stratum, mode and posterior mean agree to within 1%. The pilot shows the problem is noise-limited. The likelihood is exact, residuals sit at the noise level, and GN uncertainty is calibrated. The only remaining lever is the estimator readout. The squared-error-optimal readout under the uniform box prior is E[k|y]. It differs from the clipped mode mainly where the Gaussian likelihood is truncated by the box. A rough magnitude estimate puts about 7% of samples near a bound for each end parameter, so the aggregate effect should be about 1-3% and the boundary-stratum effect much larger. This is a mechanism-level and falsifiable prediction. The harness forward model equals the data generator. The pilot fit_report supports this (residual std 0.000995, model_mismatch=false). Paired arm P-003 (or P-005) uses the same LM transform, iterations and extra_starts, with noise_aug matched at 0. With 128 Laplace importance samples, ESS is above about 30 for interior samples. It may degrade near the bounds. Equal-quarter segments are not needed for this claim.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Single-basin test: one LM start from the prior centre reproduces multistart MLE accuracy
text: The log-space misfit has a single basin on [0.5,2]^4. Bounded LM from the prior centre alone (multistart=1, 30 iterations, mode) therefore achieves val rel_l2 within 3% of the 4-start result (pilot 0.0190) and below 0.0205. Its chi2 wrong-basin fraction is below 1%. This is a structural claim about the inverse operator. The multistart pilot converged to noise-level residuals (chi2/dof 0.94) with calibrated uncertainty, but it cannot tell whether the extra starts were needed. If one start suffices, the landscape is effectively unimodal on the box. In that case learned initializers (P-001, P-003, P-006, P-007) buy only compute, never accuracy, and the portfolio's open question 'does init matter' is settled at low cost. Harness multistart=1 starts at the prior centre, (1.25,...,1.25) in k or its log-space equivalent. 30 LM iterations suffice from the centre, since the farthest corner is about 0.7 in log-k per coordinate and cond is about 47. The forward model equals the data generator (pilot fit_report confirms this). Bound handling by projection in log space is unchanged from the ms=4 pilot.

title: Low-rank amortised inverse: MLP on unscaled PCA scores of the sensor traces still leaves a >=1.3x gap to forward-model refinement
text: Diffusion makes the noise-free sensor traces effectively low-rank (about 10 to 25 informative directions). An MLP on the top 24 raw-scale PCA scores with log targets reaches val rel_l2 in [0.03, 0.06]. That is below the 0.05 target in most of the range, but at least 1.3x worse than the best hybrid, because finite-sample estimation error at n = 3000 dominates the noise floor. This separates two explanations for any amortisation gap: input representation (800 correlated, partly noise-dominated features) vs sample size. PCA on raw-scale traces keeps the signal subspace and discards isotropic noise directions. If a gap remains with a compact representation, it is attributable to n = 3000 and to regression error. If the gap closes, amortised inference is sufficient, and is much cheaper at test time than per-sample LM. Without scaling, the leading 24 PCA directions capture the signal variance; noise (sigma = 0.001, isotropic) is spread evenly across the remaining directions torch_mlp's LayerNorm handles the unequal scale of PCA scores Log targets roughly align the squared loss with rel_l2 About 20 s runtime: 24-dimensional input, about 2400 optimiser steps

author: researcher-experimental
title: Noise-limited regime: bounded log-space MLE through the forward model should land near the CRB floor (~0.02 rel_l2)
text: The observation map is locally well-conditioned (Fisher condition number median 46.6) and sigma=0.001 is small relative to the signal. Most of the irreducible error should therefore come from measurement noise, not from model misfit or local minima. A per-sample bounded Levenberg–Marquardt MLE in log-k with a few multistarts should reach val rel_l2 within about 1.6x of the harness CRB floor (0.0195), i.e. below 0.032, clearing the 0.05 target. The competing explanation is non-convexity or multimodality of the misfit, especially in the weakly determined k1 and k4. If that is right, a large share of samples will converge to wrong basins and rel_l2 will stay well above the CRB, with a heavy-tailed per-sample error distribution. Training and test data come from the same known forward model: explicit FD, 40 points, 200 steps, known Gaussian initial condition, known i.i.d. noise. So the likelihood is exactly specified, with no simulation-fidelity gap. An exactly specified Gaussian likelihood with 4 parameters and many correlated time samples is the textbook setting where MLE approaches the CRB. A learned regressor trained on 3000 draws has to learn a 4-D inverse map from high-dimensional noisy features. That adds approximation and estimation error on top of the noise floor. The physics arm is the natural reference that every data-driven arm should be judged against. context.forward is the same simulator (grid, dt, IC, sensor indices) that generated the train/val/test features, so there is zero model discrepancy Noise is additive i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=0.001 on every reading, so least squares equals MLE The log transform makes the misfit better conditioned and keeps k positive; bounds [0.5, 2] are enforced by projection or clipping 3 multistarts x 30 LM iterations over 750 val samples fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit (4-parameter Jacobian and cheap explicit FD solves) The CRB is evaluated at 32 prior draws, so the 0.0195 floor is an estimate; near-boundary truths can make the box-constrained MLE biased but with lower variance Treat this as the canonical physics-mode arm. It absorbs P-002.

data.falsifiable_test: Run on the 750 val samples. Report overall rel_l2, per-parameter relative RMSE versus the CRB per-parameter std, and the fraction of samples whose final residual norm^2 exceeds the chi-square 99% quantile for the observation dimension (a wrong-basin indicator). The hypothesis is refuted if val rel_l2 >= 0.032, or if more than 5% of samples have residuals inconsistent with sigma=0.001, which would point to local minima or model mismatch rather than a noise limit.
data.if_fails: If residuals are chi-square-consistent but error is still above 1.6x CRB, the error comes from estimator bias or boundary effects, and an MMSE estimator (proposal 2) should help. If residuals are too large, we have local minima, so better initialization (a learned init) is the remedy. If even the best restarts misfit, the forward model does not match the data generator, which is a simulation-fidelity finding that would also undermine any physics-based arm.

title: Metric-matched estimator: a learned init plus LM refinement with a posterior-mean (MMSE) readout beats the MAP/MLE mode on rel_l2, mainly via k1 and k4 near the
text: rel_l2 is a squared-error metric, so under the known uniform box prior the Bayes-optimal point estimate is the posterior mean, not the mode. For the weakly determined k1 and k4, the posterior near the bounds 0.5 and 2.0 is truncated and skewed. The mode piles up on the bound or overshoots in log space, while the posterior mean shrinks correctly. The hybrid works in two steps. A cheap ridge regressor on log features gives a basin-correct initial guess, which removes the need for multistart. LM refinement plus importance-sampled posterior mean should then reach val rel_l2 at least 5% lower than the best pure-physics (mode) arm. The competing explanation is that the posterior is near-Gaussian and far from the bounds for almost all samples. In that case mean and mode coincide, and the gain will be under 2%, within seed noise. This is an evaluation-design argument: match the estimator to the loss. Because the prior and noise model are specified exactly, the posterior mean is computable and its benefit is directly testable against the mode. Using a learned initializer also tests a separate, data-distribution question: is a simple amortized map trained on 3000 simulated draws good enough to put LM in the right basin? If so, physics-grade accuracy can be reached with fewer forward solves than multistart needs. The uniform box prior on [0.5, 2] given in the task is the true data-generating prior for val and test, so it is valid to use it in the MMSE estimator The Laplace approximation is a good enough importance proposal; with 128 samples the effective sample size stays high when the posterior is close to Gaussian Ridge on log features is accurate enough, which seems likely since baseline rel_l2 is 0.33 and a linear map should cut that substantially, to place most samples in the global basin The compute budget allows 20 LM iterations plus 128 forward evaluations per sample for the importance weights noise model (from the simulator): additive i.i.d. That is a paired contrast on the same samples, with the estimator as the only difference.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Amortised posterior mean without forward calls: a raw-target squared-loss MLP estimates E[k|y] directly; test it against the 0.05 target and against P-004's log
text: A torch_mlp trained by squared loss on the 3000 prior-distributed noisy simulations, with an untransformed target, approximates E[k|y]. (a) It reaches val rel_l2 < 0.05 without any forward-model calls. (b) It stays at least 30% worse than the best hybrid, because finite-sample approximation error dominates the Bayes risk. (c) Its val rel_l2 is within 10% of P-004's log-target MLP, because the Jensen bias of exp(E[log k|y]) is about 1e-4 relative, which is negligible. This challenges the framing that per-sample physics inversion is needed. Simulation-based regression under squared loss is amortised Bayesian inference: its population minimiser is the posterior mean, the estimator that minimises the squared-error metric. The open question is quantitative, namely whether 3000 draws in 4-D suffice. Using the raw target makes the estimator exactly the MMSE functional, and comparing it with P-004 tests whether the theory-motivated target choice matters in practice. It does not duplicate P-004's configuration. The training features already contain i.i.d. sensor noise at sigma=0.001, so the (y, k) pairs are draws from the joint prior-times-likelihood, and no augmentation is needed for the regression target to be E[k|y]. The inverse map y -> E[k|y] is smooth on the support. Plausible: the heat solution depends analytically on k, and the posterior is concentrated, with relative spread of about 1-2%. A 4-D parameter space with 3000 draws is dense enough for a smooth regressor to resolve about 0.5% changes in k2 and k3. This is the assumption most at risk.

title: TheoremSearch: convergence of Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with bounds
text: convergence of Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least squares parameter estimation with bounds The gradient of f is Lipschitz continuous with constant L. The Hessian approximations are bounded above and below by positive constants. The sequence of parameters produced by the algorithm is bounded. The estimator converges almost surely to the true parameter as the sample size increases. This holds under specific conditions on the parameter bounds and the assumptions of a referenced theorem. The parameter values are constrained within a defined interval. The result applies to a particular estimator defined in a prior equation. The function L is bounded above and below by expressions involving the Frobenius norm of the estimated parameter matrix. The upper bound is a linear function of the squared norm plus a constant. The lower bound is the squared norm itself. The function L is bounded in probability if and only if the parameter estimate is bounded in probability. An estimable parameter is bounded.

Given a source distribution, a transformed variable is defined by scaling, shifting, and adding noise. The theorem bounds the difference between the original variable and a normalized version of the transformed variable. The bound depends on the noise magnitude and the scaling factor. Under an uncorrelated noise assumption, the bound simplifies with a smaller delta term. Under a given noise assumption, with high probability, the absolute value of a normalized sum of certain noise terms is bounded. It also includes an additional term involving the noise scale, a parameter o, and n, scaled by the square root of the logarithm of n divided by o. Under certain assumptions, there exist positive universal constants such that with high probability, the infinity norm of a scaled noise term is bounded by a constant multiple of the product of a noise parameter, the L1 norm of an undefined term, and the square root of a ratio involving sample sizes and dimensions. This bound holds uniformly for all vectors in a specified set.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: TheoremSearch: Per-feature signal-to-noise across the training set
text: Per-feature signal-to-noise across the training set After a certain training batch and epoch, the inner products between weight vector changes and the feature vector are bounded. The bound for the signal component depends on the signal-to-noise ratio and logarithmic terms. The bounds for the noise components differ based on whether the label matches the weight index. All bounds scale with the number of samples and a step size parameter. A central limit theorem holds for the signal-to-noise ratio of an estimator under unsupervised training. The scaled and centered SNR converges in distribution to a standard normal random variable. The scaling factor involves a variance term defined using specific matrix expressions. This variance term depends on the matrices and vectors defined in the assumptions. The asymptotic regularized training error for a random feature model converges to a deterministic limit involving signal and noise components. The squared norm of the minimizer also converges to a related deterministic expression. These results hold for any positive regularization parameter under proportional asymptotic growth of dimensions. The convergence is in expectation over random covariates, feature vectors, noise, and the nonlinear part of the true regression function. Under a given condition, the maximum inner products and signal strengths remain bounded by terms involving initial noise and signal magnitude during a specified time interval. The noise components from spurious features are also bounded by initial parameters and data dimension. The average training loss over iterations is bounded by the initial distance to optimal weights and a small error term. An iterate with training loss below epsilon is guaranteed within T iterations.

author: literature
title: Lemma 2 — Towards Understanding Generalization in DP-GD: A Case Study in Training Two-Layer CNNs
text: Under a given condition, the maximum inner products and signal strengths remain bounded by terms involving initial noise and signal magnitude during a specified time interval. The noise components from spurious features are also bounded by initial parameters and data dimension. The average training loss over iterations is bounded by the initial distance to optimal weights and a small error term. An iterate with training loss below epsilon is guaranteed within T iterations. Under Condition \ref {condition}, let $T^* = T_{1} + \Big \lfloor \frac {\|\bm{W} ^{(T_{1})} - \bm{W} ^{*}\|_{F}^{2}}{2\eta \epsilon } \Big \rfloor = T_{1} + \tilde {O}\left (\frac {m^{3}n}{\eta \epsilon ||\bm{\mu} ||_2^2} \right )$. Then we have \begin {itemize} \item $\max _{j,r} \langle \bm{w} _{j,r}^{(t)}, j \bm{\mu} \rangle = \tilde {O} (\sigma _0 ||\bm{\mu} ||_2)$, $\max _{j,r}\gamma _{j,r}^{(t)} = \tilde {O} (\sigma _0 ||\bm{\mu} ||_2)$, for all $T_{1} \leq t \leq T^*$. \item $\max _{j,r,i}|\underline{\rho}_{j,r,i} ^{(t)}| = \tilde {O}(\sigma _{0}\sigma _{p}\sqrt {d})$, for all $T_{1} \leq t \leq T$. \end {itemize} Besides, for all $T_{1} \leq t \leq T^*$, we have \begin {align*} &\frac {1}{t - T_{1} + 1}\sum _{s=T_{1}}^{t}L_{S}(\bm{W} ^{(s)}) \\ \leq & \frac {\|\bm{W} ^{(T_{1})} - \bm{W} ^{*}\|_{F}^{2}}{(2q-1) \eta (t - T_{1} + 1)} + \frac {\epsilon }{(2q-1)}. \end {align*} Therefore, we can find an iterate with training loss smaller than $\epsilon $ within $T$ iterations.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Single-basin test: one LM start from the prior centre reproduces multistart MLE accuracy
text: The log-space misfit has a single basin on [0.5,2]^4. Bounded LM from the prior centre alone (multistart=1, 30 iterations, mode) therefore achieves val rel_l2 within 3% of the 4-start result (pilot 0.0190) and below 0.0205. Its chi2 wrong-basin fraction is below 1%. This is a structural claim about the inverse operator. The multistart pilot converged to noise-level residuals (chi2/dof 0.94) with calibrated uncertainty, but it cannot tell whether the extra starts were needed. If one start suffices, the landscape is effectively unimodal on the box. In that case learned initializers (P-001, P-003, P-006, P-007) buy only compute, never accuracy, and the portfolio's open question 'does init matter' is settled at low cost. Harness multistart=1 starts at the prior centre, (1.25,...,1.25) in k or its log-space equivalent. 30 LM iterations suffice from the centre, since the farthest corner is about 0.7 in log-k per coordinate and cond is about 47. The forward model equals the data generator (pilot fit_report confirms this). Bound handling by projection in log space is unchanged from the ms=4 pilot. noise model (from the simulator): additive i.i.d. Gaussian on every sensor reading; the likelihood must match it Treat the single-basin claim as 'every sample's ms=1 solution matches its ms=4 solution to within 0.1 GN-std'. This is directly checkable and stronger than an aggregate comparison.

data.falsifiable_test:
Compare against the ms=4 physics run (P-005 or pilot) on identical val samples.

The hypothesis is falsified under either of these outcomes:
(a) rel_l2(ms=1) exceeds 1.03 x rel_l2(ms=4), or exceeds 0.0205;
(b) more than 1% of samples have a scaled residual above the chi2_m 99% quantile.

Samples that stop at a k1/k4 bound with a chi2-consistent residual are reported separately as ridge/bound cases.
data.if_fails: If ms=1 loses accuracy and shows high-chi2 samples, the landscape has secondary basins. Initialization then matters, and the learned-init hybrids gain a genuine accuracy rationale. Inspecting the failing truths, for example low k2 with extreme k1, locates the non-injective region. If accuracy drops but residuals stay chi2-consistent, the failure is ridge-plus-bound, not multimodality.

title: Mode twin of P-014: ridge/log init + LM20, estimator=mode, paired against P-014's posterior_mean
text: This arm uses P-014's init and LM settings with estimator=mode (bounded log-space MLE). It reaches val rel_l2 < 0.0205. On the paired per-sample contrast with P-014, the posterior_mean improves aggregate rel_l2 by 0% to 3% relative. On the shared boundary stratum (true k1 or k4 within 2 GN-std of 0.5 or 2.0), the improvement exceeds 10% relative. rel_l2 is a squared-error metric, so the posterior mean is Bayes-optimal under the uniform prior and the mode is not. The noise is small (sigma = 0.001), the Fisher condition number is about 47, and the CRB rel std is 0.5% to 2%. In that regime the posterior is near-Gaussian and narrow, so mode and mean coincide to first order away from the box. They separate only where the box truncates the posterior, and that is most likely for k1 and k4. A contrast that is matched in everything except the readout isolates this mechanism. P-014 predicts a gain of at least 5%; P-009 and this arm predict 0% to 3%. This pair adjudicates directly between those predictions. context.forward matches the data generator (no model error) Noise is i.i.d. author: researcher-ml
title: Amortised inverse on information-preserving PCA-48 scores: below target but at least 1.3x the hybrid, with the gap concentrated in k1/k4
text: An MLP on the top 48 unscaled PCA scores of the raw sensor traces, with log targets, trained on all 3000 samples, reaches val rel_l2 in [0.025, 0.05]. That is below the 0.05 target but at least 1.3x worse than the best hybrid. The excess over the CRB is largest for k1 and k4: their per-parameter rel error divided by CRB rel std exceeds that of k2 and k3. The gap is due to finite-sample regression error, not to the representation, provided the projected-Fisher pilot shows that PCA-48 retains at least 99% of the information. This separates two explanations for any amortisation gap: input representation and sample size. Isotropic noise makes unscaled PCA noise-whitened, and r=48 is chosen to keep the low-amplitude k1/k4 directions. A remaining gap is then attributable to regression error at n=3000. The 300-sample pilot (0.066) against a full-data run gives a two-point learning-curve check on that attribution. PCA-48 retains at least 99% of the Fisher information for every parameter (to be verified by the projected-Fisher pilot) torch_mlp's LayerNorm handles the unequal scales of the PCA scores Log targets roughly align the squared loss with rel_l2 Runtime about 40 to 50 s on CPU

author: researcher-experimental
title: Noise-limited regime: bounded log-space MLE through the forward model should land near the CRB floor (~0.02 rel_l2)
text: The observation map is locally well-conditioned (Fisher condition number median 46.6) and sigma=0.001 is small relative to the signal. Most of the irreducible error should therefore come from measurement noise, not from model misfit or local minima. A per-sample bounded Levenberg–Marquardt MLE in log-k with a few multistarts should reach val rel_l2 within about 1.6x of the harness CRB floor (0.0195), i.e. below 0.032, clearing the 0.05 target. The competing explanation is non-convexity or multimodality of the misfit, especially in the weakly determined k1 and k4. If that is right, a large share of samples will converge to wrong basins and rel_l2 will stay well above the CRB, with a heavy-tailed per-sample error distribution. Training and test data come from the same known forward model: explicit FD, 40 points, 200 steps, known Gaussian initial condition, known i.i.d. noise. So the likelihood is exactly specified, with no simulation-fidelity gap. An exactly specified Gaussian likelihood with 4 parameters and many correlated time samples is the textbook setting where MLE approaches the CRB. A learned regressor trained on 3000 draws has to learn a 4-D inverse map from high-dimensional noisy features. That adds approximation and estimation error on top of the noise floor. My point estimate is 0.032-0.047, about 1.6-2.4x the CRB floor of 0.0195. This challenges the framing that per-sample physics inversion is required. Squared-loss regression on joint (k, y) draws is amortised Bayesian inference, and its population minimiser is the MMSE estimator for the metric. Removing standardisation keeps the noise geometry isotropic, so any remaining gap to the hybrids is attributable to sample scarcity or approximation rather than input-scaling artefacts. That makes this arm the clean forward-free comparator for the hybrid family. Training features contain i.i.d. noise at sigma=0.001, so the (y, k) pairs are draws from prior times likelihood. No augmentation is needed. With scaler='none', LayerNorm after the first linear layer compensates for the small absolute input scale, so optimisation is not crippled. This is a risk; a failure would show as rel_l2 near or above the pilot value. y -> E[k|y] is smooth on the support, because the heat solution depends analytically on k and the posterior is concentrated at about 1-2% relative. 3000 draws in 4-D suffice to resolve about 0.5% changes in k2 and k3 to within about 2x the CRB. assumptions: Training features contain i.i.d. noise at sigma=0.001, so the (y, k) pairs are draws from prior times likelihood. No augmentation is needed.

With scaler='none', LayerNorm after the first linear layer compensates for the small absolute input scale, so optimisation is not crippled. This is a risk; a failure would show as rel_l2 near or above the pilot value.
y -> E[k|y] is smooth on the support, because the heat solution depends analytically on k and the posterior is concentrated at about 1-2% relative.
3000 draws in 4-D suffice to resolve about 0.5% changes in k2 and k3 to within about 2x the CRB. This is the assumption most at risk.

title: supported: Noise-limited regime: bounded log-space MLE through the forward model should land near the CRB floor (~0.02 rel_l2)
text: The observation map is locally well-conditioned (Fisher condition number median 46.6) and sigma=0.001 is small relative to the signal. Most of the irreducible error should therefore come from measurement noise, not from model misfit or local minima. A per-sample bounded Levenberg–Marquardt MLE in log-k with a few multistarts should reach val rel_l2 within about 1.6x of the harness CRB floor (0.0195), i.e. below 0.032, clearing the 0.05 target. The competing explanation is non-convexity or multimodality of the misfit, especially in the weakly determined k1 and k4. If that is right, a large share of samples will converge to wrong basins and rel_l2 will stay well above the CRB, with a heavy-tailed per-sample error distribution. prediction {"metric": "rel_l2", "op": "<", "value": 0.032}: val rel_l2 = 0.019325 vs predicted < 0.032

assumptions: context.forward is the same simulator (grid, dt, IC, sensor indices) that generated the train/val/test features, so there is zero model discrepancy
Noise is additive i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=0.001 on every reading, so least squares equals MLE
The log transform makes the misfit better conditioned and keeps k positive; bounds [0.5, 2] are enforced by projection or clipping
3 multistarts x 30 LM iterations over 750 val samples fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit (4-parameter Jacobian and cheap explicit FD solves)
The CRB is evaluated at 32 prior draws, so the 0.0195 floor is an estimate; near-boundary truths can make the box-constrained MLE biased but with lower variance
Treat this as the canonical physics-mode arm. It absorbs P-002.

Asymptotic CRLB attainment (ts:thm:26986930, 27031792) does not apply with box constraints. Truncation lets MSE fall below CRB, as the pilot hints. 'Within 1.6x of CRB' should be 'within [0.9, 1.1]x of the val-matched CRB'.
